newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Guatemala army tracking down gang linked to rebels.
newsitem.headline: Guatemala army tracking down gang linked to rebels.

text.p: Guatemalan troops were pursuing a newly emerged armed band that claims status as a guerrilla army and has been blamed for recent armed robberies in southwestern Guatemala, officials said on Tuesday.
The army has denied reports that a new guerrilla force has emerged since this would jeopardise the delicate peace process aimed at ending a 36 year-long civil war.

"We are mobilising units to carry out the full identification of (the gang). These people are common criminals. We have not established any link with guerrilla units," army spokesman Col. Otto Noack told Reuters.

For several weeks farmers in small towns around the southwestern city of Coatepeque have reported a string of armed robberies that they blame on a heavily armed group that identifies itself as a guerrilla front.

The violence peaked on Friday when a 76-year-old rubber farmer and his employee were shot to death during a robbery. Witnesses blamed 15 men dressed in olive green claiming to be from the Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unit (URNG).
The URNG, a group of four guerrilla factions that have been fighting the government for 36 years, was in the final phases of delicate peace talks with the government.

A definitive peace agreement was scheduled for Dec. 29. But if bonafide guerrillas were involved in the attacks it could crumble five years of hard-won negotiations to end a war that has left an estimated 100,000 dead and 40,000 missing.

URNG commander Pablo Monsanto, in exile in Mexico City, was quoted by Guatemala's major daily newspaper Prensa Libre as saying the URNG had nothing to do with the farm robberies. As part of ongoing peace negotiations the URNG declared a ceasefire this year and there have been no clashes between the URNG and the army for months.
Despite army and guerrilla assurances that the new group was merely criminal, Guatemala's traditionally ultra-conservative agricultural sector is not convinced.

Humberto Pretti, president of the Agricultural Chamber, said the gangs who have robbed coffee, farm payroll clerks, vehicles and farm houses clearly have military training. he also told Reuters the gang that sometimes calls itself the Popular Revolutionary Army (EPRG) has sophisticated automatic weapons.
